title: The little ones
hook: Jesus warns fiercely against harming children (Matthew 18:6)

segments.voice: Yesterday, where churches disagree today, and the tradition's own advice for disagreeing: speak the truth in love, and stay at the table. Your line was love in disagreement. Did you get to listen before you answered? Day one thousand two hundred nineteen.

The disciples are arguing about rank. They come to Jesus with the question straight out: who is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven? You can almost hear each of them hoping. Matthew says Jesus calls a little child over and sets the child in the middle of them. No speech yet. Just a small person standing in a circle of grown men who were, a minute ago, comparing themselves. Then Jesus says that unless they become like this child, they won't enter the kingdom at all. And then comes a warning with no softness in it. Today: the little ones.

Here it is, in the King James Bible: "But whoso shall offend one of these little ones which believe in me, it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea." A millstone was the heavy stone for grinding grain. Jesus is saying: better to sink to the bottom of the sea than to do this. The word offend there doesn't mean hurt someone's feelings. The Greek is about making someone stumble, setting a trap in their path. To cause a child to fall, in body or in faith, is what he warns against. A few verses later he adds: "Take heed that ye despise not one of these little ones; for I say unto you, That in heaven their angels do always behold the face of my Father which is in heaven." Children, in this picture, are not small and forgettable. They have someone watching in the highest court there is. In Mark's Gospel, when the disciples try to shoo parents and children away, Jesus is indignant: "Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not." Suffer there means allow. These words have a hard edge for churches today. Churches have had to face abuse within their own walls, and the failure to protect children. Some now answer this chapter with practical things: background checks, two adults in every room, clear ways to report, and listening to survivors. Jesus didn't put the child at the edge of the circle. He put the child in the middle.

Here's the practice: keep one child safe. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one child you're connected to: your own, a niece or nephew, a neighbor's kid, a student, a child at church. Picture them in the middle of the circle, where Jesus put the child. Then ask a plain question: what would make them a little safer this week? A seat belt checked. A screen setting changed. An adult who listens. Knowing who to call if something seems wrong. Pick one. If you pray, you can pray for that child by name. The bell holds the time.
The little ones. Jesus's name for children, and for the small and trusting, set in the middle and fiercely protected in Matthew 18.
Your line: protect the little ones. Today, do the one thing you picked to keep a child a little safer, and do it before evening. Day one thousand two hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: Churches teach Jesus's care for children in Sunday school and preaching, and some congregations now train volunteers in child safeguarding, require background checks, and keep two adults with children at all times.

original.note: Greek, Matthew 18:6: causes to stumble; the King James Bible says offend.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus was gentle with children, so this is a soft passage.
what it means: it's a fierce warning: better a millstone and the sea than to make a little one stumble.
what a scholar hears: the verse says little ones "which believe in me," so some readers hear humble believers of any age in it, not children only.

notes: Matthew 18:6 speaks of 'these little ones which believe in me'; interpreters differ on whether 'little ones' means children only or also humble believers. The word segment names both; confirm.
Abuse in churches is named honestly but generally, without naming any church, number or case; confirm tone and that safeguarding examples are fair.
